opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I wasn't certain at first. It was more a hypothesis that we had to test very quickly.

The signal came from the Taichi days. Taichi was an open-source programming language for graphics and simulation, and through that community we talked to a lot of people: game developers, indie creators, people doing 3D printing, VFX folks. Again and again we heard the same pain point. Writing fast code wasn't their bottleneck. Content was. Making a decent 3D asset could take an artist days or even weeks, and for a small studio or a solo developer that's a huge cost. So the demand was clearly there. The question was whether AI-generated models were good enough that someone would actually pull out a credit card.

The way we got more confident was very practical. We shipped something early, even though the quality wasn't perfect, and watched what people did with it. When people kept coming back, used the models in real projects, and some started paying without us pushing very hard, that told us more than any survey. With open source, people love you, but love doesn't equal revenue. With a product that saves someone a week of work, the value is very concrete, and it's easy for them to do the math.

Another thing I learned from Taichi is that a great technology by itself doesn't make a business. You need to find the person whose problem is painful enough that they'll pay to make it go away. For us that turned out to be creators who need lots of 3D assets but don't have the time, budget, or modeling skills to make all of them by hand. Once we saw that clearly, I felt much more sure we were on the right track.

r001.rationale: The response identifies whether users would pay for AI-generated models, and distinguishes that value from Taichi, the open-source software.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I wasn't certain. I don't think anyone building something like that can be certain at the start.

What I had was a lot of signal from Taichi. Taichi was open source, and we had tens of thousands of users writing simulations and graphics code with it. And the thing I kept noticing was that people weren't just using it for research. They were building things, and they kept asking us, "Can you host this? Can I just give you a description and get something back?" The barrier for them was never the compiler. It was everything around it.

So when we started thinking about models, specifically generative models for 3D, the bet wasn't really "will people pay for a model." The bet was "there's a huge gap between what artists and developers want to make and how much time it takes to make it." Modeling a single asset by hand can take days. If you can turn that into minutes, that's not a nice-to-have, that's a real cost line on someone's budget. Studios already pay for that labor. We're just changing who, or what, does it.

The other thing I learned from Taichi is that willingness to pay usually comes down to whether the output goes straight into production. If the model gives you something you have to rebuild from scratch, nobody pays. If it gives you something you can drop into Blender or Unity and actually ship, then it's just a question of price. So most of our effort went into that last mile, not the demo.

And then, frankly, you find out by charging. We put a price on it early and watched who stayed. That's the only real certainty you get.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes Taichi, the open-source software, from a later generative 3D modeling product, but it does not identify users’ willingness to pay for models within the previous product. It even says the initial bet was not really whether people would pay for a model.

astra-6.text: I wouldn’t say I was certain. People using your software is one signal, but it doesn’t necessarily mean they’ll pay for models. The real question is whether those models solve a problem well enough to justify the cost—whether they save users time or help them do something they couldn’t do before. Until people actually pay, it’s still a hypothesis.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes using the software from paying for models and explicitly frames willingness to pay as depending on whether the models justify their cost.

sol-6.1.text: I wouldn’t say we were certain. With our previous software, we saw that people could get excited about the technology without necessarily wanting to pay for it. So the question was: are we solving a problem that matters enough to their work? For models, our hypothesis was that if we could save users a meaningful amount of time creating something they needed, there would be a reason to pay. But that was still a hypothesis—you have to put the product in front of people and see whether they actually do.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts users’ reluctance to pay for the previous software with the hypothesis that they would pay for models that save them meaningful time.
